title: Is it a 'full stop' or a 'period'? | PUNCTUATION

entries.note: From Latin [[from:pungere]], to prick or pierce; first used for marks on Hebrew texts, it replaced [[see:pointing]] during the Renaissance fashion for foreign terms.
Given as a relative of [[same-root:punctuation]], from Latin pungere, to prick.
Given as a relative of [[same-root:punctuation]], from Latin pungere, to prick.
Given as a relative of [[same-root:punctuation]], from Latin pungere, to prick.
Given as a relative of [[same-root:punctuation]], from Latin pungere, to prick.
Related to [[same-root:punctuation]]; in typography, the smallest unit of measurement, matching the width of an [[see:em]] in a font of that size.
The older English word for the little marks used in writing, displaced by [[see:punctuation]] during the Renaissance.
Dots and marks used to notate Psalms so they could be sung or chanted in a set rhythm; one of the earliest English contexts for [[see:punctuation]].
Origin uncertain: perhaps from the Gregorian [[from?:punctus interrogativus]], a hieroglyph of a cat's tail, or Q stacked above O, abbreviating Latin [[from?:quaestio]].
A Gregorian chant mark, a jagged rising line like a lightning flash over a dot, telling chanters to rise then stop; the favoured ancestor of the [[gave?:question mark]].
Supposedly from Latin [[from?:io]], abbreviated with I over O; Rob's British term, versus Jess's American [[see:exclamation point]].
Exclamation means to cry out in Latin; the American name, contrasted with the British [[see:exclamation mark]].
A name briefly used for the [[see:exclamation mark]] in the 1800s, also used by printers.
Printers' rude alliterative name for the [[see:exclamation mark]], alluded to but not said; compared with the cat's-tail theory of the [[see:question mark]].
The American term, from Greek [[from:periodos]], the longest pause in [[see:Aristophanes of Byzantium]]'s three-dot system, denoting the span of the sentence.
The British name for the [[see:period]], which Jess finds firmer and Rob says tells you better what it does.
Scholar at the Library of Alexandria credited with marking texts with three dots for pauses, named periodos, [[see:comma]] and [[see:colon]].
Greek for something cut off, also a clause or line of poetry; first a short pause dot, its mark later developed from the slash-like [[from:virgule]].
From a Greek word for limb or member, a part of a verse; one of the three pause marks of [[see:Aristophanes of Byzantium]].
Roman who said only the rhythm of a text should guide reading aloud, which is why the Romans dropped the Greek pause marks.
A long forward-slash mark that shrank into the modern [[see:comma]]; French and Italian speakers recognise it as their word for comma.
Literally to write beside, from a medieval break mark; from the 17th century it meant an actual break in printed text. Mangled into [[gave:pilcrow]].
The paragraph symbol, a corruption of [[from:paragraph]] via Old French pelagraphe and English pylcraft; the original mark was the [[see:capitulum]].
Means header; a red C-like mark added later by another scribe, whose omitted gap gave paragraph indentation; same origin as [[same-root:chapter]] and [[same-root:capitulate]].
Shares its origin with [[same-root:capitulum]].
To bow your head, sharing its origin with [[same-root:capitulum]].
One of many head-related words from the same source as [[same-root:capitulum]].
One of many head-related words from the same source as [[same-root:capitulum]].
Comes in three types, the [[see:hyphen]], [[see:en dash]] and [[see:em dash]], the subject of one of Jess's most popular videos.
The shortest dash, joining compounds; Greek for under one, as it was once a crescent written beneath compound parts.
The middle-length dash, standing for through in spans; named after the [[from:en]], a typographic unit.
The longest dash, for sharp breaks, insertions and interruptions; named after the [[from:em]], and used heavily by [[see:Emily Dickinson]].
A typographic unit, usually half an [[see:em]], loosely linked to the width of a lowercase n.
A typographic unit linked to the printing block for M, and more reliably to a font's [[see:point]] size.
The small printing stamps bearing letters, whose widths Rob suggests gave the [[see:en dash]] and [[see:em dash]] their lengths.
Poet whose frequent [[see:em dash]]es add meaning through jarring cut-offs and implied omissions.
Means to come short, suggesting an unfinished thought; also marks omissions in quotes. [[see:Shakespeare]] never used it.
Never used the [[see:ellipsis]], though it had been invented by his time.
A question mark and exclamation mark overlaid, proposed by [[see:Martin K. Speckter]] for surprised rhetorical questions; uses [[see:bang]] for the exclamation mark.
A double-meaning word for the exclamation mark, used in [[see:interrobang]].
Proposed the [[see:interrobang]] as a tool for copywriters.
Placed around words online for ironic emphasis, one of the modern ways of signalling sarcasm.
Ends a sentence online to flag sarcasm, echoing HTML and XML closing tags.
A backwards question mark from the 1500s, first for open questions and later rhetorical ones, which faded away; resembles the [[see:Arabic question mark]].
Faces backwards because Arabic is read right to left, so it looks like the [[see:percontation point]].
Begins Spanish sentences, as recommended by the [[see:Royal Spanish Academy]] in 1754; [[see:John Wilkins]] first proposed it in 1668 to mark irony.
Recommended opening inverted marks in 1754, though they weren't fully adopted until the 19th century.
English clergyman who proposed the [[see:inverted exclamation point]] in 1668, for sentence ends to denote irony or sarcasm.
Quotation marks around something that isn't a quote, implying irony.
Text leaning like a left-hander's [[see:italics]]; possible on computers but never used, with sarcasm proposed as a use.
Lean as if handwritten by a right-hander, and can already convey disingenuousness in the right context.
A saggy, whip-like backwards question mark proposed by [[see:Alcanter de Brahm]] to denote verbal irony.
French poet who proposed the [[see:point d'ironie]].
French writer, died 1998, whose 1960s book proposed new marks including the [[see:love point]] and [[see:doubt mark]].
Two question marks facing each other and sharing a dot, as if about to kiss, proposed by [[see:Hervé Bazin]] to denote emotion.
A stylised, pointy question mark proposed by [[see:Hervé Bazin]].
Greek for turning away, showing an omitted letter; the possessive marks a dropped E from Old and Middle English -es, not a contraction of his.
The comma before and in a list, apparently named after Oxford University's style; omitting it can cause ambiguity, though the hosts favour clarity over rules.
A [[see:ligature]] of Latin [[from:et]], from and per se and; once recited as a letter after Z, and found in Pompeii graffiti.
Several letters cast on one printing piece; Rob suggests the [[see:ampersand]] is arguably one, and it gave us [[gave:logo]].
Shortened from [[from:logogram]], a single cast piece such as one printing the whole word Google.
Joined letters like the E and T forming the [[see:ampersand]], which Jess scribbles in handwriting.
Latin for and the others, once written as an [[see:ampersand]] followed by C, hence the ampersand's long name.
The T is most likely short for [[from?:tittle]], the dot on an i or j.
The dot on an i or j, added so i could be told apart from u, m and n; paired with [[see:jot]] in Matthew 5:18.
Originally the least part of anything, later a short written mark like the Greek [[see:iota]]; also an old English name for J, reflecting its Y sound.
The smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, given as an example of a [[see:jot]].
Symbols replacing a censored swear word, also called an [[see:obscenicon]]; popularised by [[see:Mort Walker]], probably imitative of [[see:growl]] and [[see:scrawl]], with -x echoing [[see:comix]].
An alternative name for a [[see:grawlix]].
Cartoonist who introduced the [[see:grawlix]] to wide readership in The Lexicon of Comicana, which names many comic symbols.
An editor of [[see:Mort Walker]]'s who coined several such terms and may have written about the [[see:grawlix]] for This Week magazine in the 1960s.
A word [[see:grawlix]] perhaps imitates.
A word [[see:grawlix]] perhaps imitates.
A spelling of comics in early and mid-1900s cartoonist culture, perhaps echoed in the ending of [[see:grawlix]].
[[see:Mort Walker]]'s term for curved lines drawn beside a character's excitedly waving limbs.
[[see:Mort Walker]]'s term for curved lines drawn beside a character's excitedly waving limbs.
[[see:Mort Walker]]'s term for the clouds left when a character swiftly darts away, or [[see:absquatulate]]s.
One of Rob's favourite words, used to describe a character darting away in [[see:briffits]].
[[see:Mort Walker]]'s term for wavy lines rising from something hot, steamy or stinky.
[[see:Mort Walker]]'s term for sweat droplets around a nervous or hard-working character.
[[see:Mort Walker]]'s term for starbursts and birds circling the head of a character who's been hit.
